extracted.intended_audience: readers of juvenile/young-adult domestic fiction (general audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter excerpt from a juvenile/young-adult domestic fiction novel (Blue Bonnet) focusing on holiday social life, manners, gift-giving, and domestic crafts. Contains dialogue that includes practical advice on shopping, wrapping, crocheting, and clubroom norms embedded in the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christmas shopping planning (make a list)
rubrics_metrics.description: “You must make a list before leaving home, putting down the names of all the persons you intend giving presents to, and opposite the name the gift you have decided upon.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start planning early (Miss Lucinda: “I began last Spring!”). Kitty’s method: make a recipient→gift list before you leave; be prepared for practical failures (leave or lose the list as Kitty jokingly notes), but the list is the organizing principle for efficient gift-buying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrap and label gifts in the store to avoid confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Kitty’s instruction: “As soon as you’ve bought your present you must wrap it up in tissue paper and tie it prettily with ribbon and label it--Right there in the store!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to avoid last-minute confusion when assembling gifts at home. Practical steps implied: wrap immediately, use tissue paper and ribbon, attach a clear label naming recipient. (Humorous aside in text: some still lose or misplace lists afterward.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Crocheting: practice stitch and correct mistakes by unraveling
rubrics_metrics.description: Grandmother’s teaching and advice: practice the stitch a little before starting the regular work; if wrong, ‘Better unravel that and start afresh.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with a simpler project if you are a novice (Grandmother suggests starting simpler than a shoulder shawl). Avoid the shortcut of simply breaking off; undoing (unraveling) and restarting produces better results. Also attend to technique/posture (Sarah corrects holding the finger out: ‘You shouldn’t hold your finger out like that! You’ll get the habit.’).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clubroom organization and safety norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of the clubroom: “There was nothing breakable--in the ordinary sense--and there were no curtains at the four windows... the center table, the wide lounge... the quaint medley of chairs... on club days, a bright fire burned in the deep fireplace, behind the tall wire screen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied standards for a girls’ club space: make it comfortable and informal (cushions, lounge), remove fragile items, avoid drapery that could be hazardous near an open fire, use a screen for fireplace safety, and keep furnishings that tolerate active use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hosting & family social etiquette at formal gatherings
rubrics_metrics.description: Various remarks about duty, respect, and propriety: treat visiting relatives seriously (‘they are to be taken seriously’); punctuality and consideration for hosts (Aunt Lucinda criticizes keeping Uncle Cliff waiting as ‘wanting in proper respect to Mr. Ashe’); consult elders about unusual attire (‘Suppose we say, not without consulting your grandmother or me’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied social standards for formal family occasions: observe punctuality, show proper respect to hosts and elders, be mindful of family traditions and symbolism (names, dress), and consult senior family members before making conspicuous departures from expected dress or behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community gift/charity-box practice (what to include and collaborative boxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blue Bonnet and friends’ plan: send a Christmas box to Carita (the missionary-box girl); ideas like putting ‘something for each of the boys’ and making a communal ‘We are Seven’ box with letters from each girl (‘And all write a letter to put in it’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines for charitable gift boxes: include small items appropriate to recipients (e.g., a knife for boys mentioned in the letter), include a personal letter from the sender(s), coordinate contributions among a group for a richer box, and consider practical repairs or alterations (the recipient mentions a dress needing a tuck).
